items.title: Everything Moves
items.question: What does the Buddhist teaching of impermanence say about all conditioned things?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Nothing conditioned persists unchanged, from objects to moods to the self.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is everything changes. Recognising this applies to pleasant and painful states alike is the heart of the teaching.
items.lessonContent:
All formed things are in motion.
Nothing lasts in fixed form.
Apply this to pleasant and painful states.
Notice change rather than resist it.
Share this: observe one thing you assumed would stay the same.

items.title: Nothing Lasts
items.question: What is the direct implication of impermanence for the things we rely on?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Whatever depends on conditions will eventually dissolve when those conditions change.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is nothing is permanent. Relying on the transient as if it were stable sets up disappointment.
items.lessonContent:
Conditioned things depend on causes.
When causes shift, the thing shifts.
Do not build on the assumption of stability.
Notice what you treat as fixed.
Share this: name one thing you assume will always be there.

items.title: Cause of Pain
items.question: In Buddhist thought, what is the main source of suffering?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Grasping at what changes inevitably brings grief when the change arrives.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is attachment causes suffering. The trouble lies not in caring but in grasping at what cannot be held.
items.lessonContent:
Grasping creates its own grief.
Loss is inevitable for held things.
Distinguish care from gripping.
Loosen the hold, keep the care.
Share this: notice one thing you hold too tightly.

items.title: Opening the Hand
items.question: What practice does the teaching of impermanence encourage toward what we hold?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Releasing the grip reduces the suffering that loss would otherwise bring.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is letting go. This is not indifference but a lighter, less fearful hold on what is precious.
items.lessonContent:
Release is a skill, not a loss.
A light grip enjoys without fearing.
Loosening differs from not caring.
Practise release in small things.
Share this: release one small expectation today.

items.title: Only Here
items.question: Where does Buddhist practice say experience can actually be met?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Only this moment can be attended to, since the past is gone and the future has not arrived.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the present moment. Dwelling on what has passed or might come spends attention on what cannot be touched.
items.lessonContent:
Only the present can be met.
The past is memory; the future is imagination.
Bring attention back to now.
Notice how often it wanders.
Share this: return your attention to the present once this hour.

items.title: Without Gripping
items.question: What attitude toward experience does the practice of non-attachment describe?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. One engages with experience without grasping, allowing things to come and go.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is non-attachment. It is not coldness but freedom from the grip that turns loss into suffering.
items.lessonContent:
Engage without gripping.
Let things come and go.
Calm is not coldness.
Practise allowing, not forcing.
Share this: engage fully in one activity without demanding a result.

items.title: The Constant Change
items.question: What is the name of the Buddhist doctrine that all things are in flux?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The doctrine holds that change is the fundamental feature of all conditioned experience.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is impermanence. Seeing it clearly loosens the grip that turns loss into pain.
items.lessonContent:
Change is not an interruption.
It is the baseline condition.
Accepting this reduces resistance.
Notice flux rather than freeze it.
Share this: note one change happening right now that you usually overlook.

items.title: Holding On
items.question: What term describes the mental grip that seeks to keep a changing thing fixed?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The grip intensifies pain because it fights the nature of what it holds.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is clinging. It is the tension between wanting permanence and living in a changing world.
items.lessonContent:
The grip fights reality.
Resistance increases suffering.
Notice the moment of holding on.
Relax the fist, keep the heart.
Share this: catch yourself gripping one expectation today.

items.title: Neither Extreme
items.question: What path does Buddhist teaching recommend between indulgence and harsh asceticism?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The balanced path avoids both self-indulgence and self-torment.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the middle way. Extremes of pleasure and denial both distract from clear seeing.
items.lessonContent:
Avoid both indulgence and denial.
Balance supports steady attention.
Extremes consume energy.
Choose the sustainable path.
Share this: find a middle point in one area where you swing between extremes.

items.title: Second Sting
items.question: In the parable of the two arrows, what does the second arrow represent?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The first arrow is unavoidable pain, while the second is the suffering we add through resistance.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the second arrow. Recognising the added layer gives a chance to put the bow down.
items.lessonContent:
Pain and suffering are distinct.
The first is given; the second is added.
Response can be changed.
Notice the extra layer.
Share this: separate one pain from the story you added to it.

items.title: Components of Self
items.question: What does Buddhist analysis divide a person into to show there is no fixed core?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Breaking a person into changing components undermines the idea of a permanent self.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the five aggregates. Each component is impermanent, so nothing unchanging remains to call the self.
items.lessonContent:
Analysing a whole into parts reveals flux.
Components change; the composite changes.
Search for a permanent core and find none.
Look closely and the fixed thing dissolves.
Share this: break one thing you call solid into its changing parts.

items.title: Lack of Fixed Nature
items.question: What does the Buddhist term for the absence of independent, fixed essence describe?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Things lack an independent essence and arise only through conditions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is emptiness. It does not mean nothing exists but that nothing exists on its own.
items.lessonContent:
Things depend on conditions to be.
No thing stands alone.
Empty of fixed essence, not of reality.
See relations rather than isolated objects.
Share this: trace the conditions that make one everyday object possible.

items.title: Woven Together
items.question: What principle holds that all things depend on and shape one another?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Nothing arises in isolation, so each thing is bound to countless others.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is interdependence. Seeing the web reduces the illusion of separate, independent selves and things.
items.lessonContent:
No thing exists alone.
Every part depends on others.
Notice the web behind one simple object.
Separateness is a useful fiction.
Share this: trace one meal back through several dependencies.

items.title: Sanskrit Flux
items.question: What is the traditional Pali or Sanskrit term for the truth of impermanence?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The term names the teaching that all conditioned things are in constant change.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is anitya. The Pali form anicca expresses the same insight about universal flux.
items.lessonContent:
Traditional terms carry centuries of thought.
Learn the vocabulary of a discipline.
Original words often resist neat translation.
Connect a term to its practice.
Share this: learn one term from a tradition you find interesting.

items.title: Subtle Unease
items.question: What is the Buddhist term for the unsatisfactoriness or unease woven through experience?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The term points to a subtle unease that even pleasant experiences carry because they cannot last.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is dukkha. It is not only dramatic suffering but a pervasive lack of final satisfaction.
items.lessonContent:
Unease can be subtle, not only dramatic.
Even pleasure carries incompleteness.
Name the feeling accurately.
Understanding precedes release.
Share this: notice one subtle unease that comes with a pleasant thing.

items.title: Pleasure Fades
items.question: Why does grasping at pleasant experiences lead to suffering, according to the teaching?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Pleasure passes, so demanding that it stay guarantees disappointment.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is clinging to pleasure. Enjoyment is not the problem; insisting on its permanence is.
items.lessonContent:
Enjoy without demanding permanence.
Pleasant states pass by nature.
The demand for more brings tension.
Relax the requirement.
Share this: enjoy one pleasant moment without trying to extend it.

items.title: Seeking Stability
items.question: What is the error of treating a changing situation as though it were fixed and will last?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Treating the impermanent as permanent builds expectations that reality will break.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is grasping at permanence. The misperception, not the situation, creates the difficulty.
items.lessonContent:
Misperception creates friction.
Expectations meet a changing world.
Adjust the assumption, not just the demand.
See things as they are.
Share this: check one assumption that something will stay the same.

items.title: Raft Parable
items.question: In the parable of the raft, what does the teaching say should happen to the raft after crossing?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The teaching is used to cross, then released, showing that even good tools are not to be clutched.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is abandon the raft. Holding on to the method once it has done its job turns a help into a burden.
items.lessonContent:
Tools are for a purpose.
Release the tool once it has served.
Good means can become attachments.
Let go even of useful things.
Share this: name one useful habit you might have outgrown.

items.title: Loose Hold
items.question: What describes engaging with life fully while relaxing the tendency to grasp?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. One can act wholeheartedly without demanding that outcomes stay fixed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is non-clinging. Effort continues while the anxious grip fades.
items.lessonContent:
Full effort without a desperate grip.
Act well, release the outcome.
Calm and engagement coexist.
Practise effort with ease.
Share this: give your best to one task and then let the result be.

items.title: Meeting Loss
items.question: What skill does the teaching of impermanence help develop when something ends?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Accepting that things end allows grief without the added torment of denial.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is accepting loss. Acceptance does not remove sadness but it removes the fight against reality.
items.lessonContent:
Loss is part of change.
Acceptance reduces the added pain.
Grief and denial are different.
Let feelings pass through.
Share this: acknowledge one ending without trying to reverse it.

items.title: Brief Things
items.question: What quality of experience does impermanence reveal when we look closely?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Seeing how quickly all things pass can deepen appreciation rather than despair.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the ephemeral nature of things. Realising their short span often makes present moments more precious.
items.lessonContent:
Shortness can sharpen appreciation.
Noticing brevity changes how we hold things.
Transience is not only a loss.
See the value in the fleeting.
Share this: appreciate one fleeting thing before it passes.

items.title: Allowing Space
items.question: What attitude lets things unfold without constant interference or control?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Allowing things to unfold reduces the strain of trying to control the uncontrollable.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is letting things be. It is not passivity but a wise sense of what is worth effort.
items.lessonContent:
Some things need effort; others need space.
Forcing deepens resistance.
Discern the difference.
Allow what you cannot steer.
Share this: stop controlling one thing that does not need it.

items.title: Never the Same
items.question: Which metaphor compares a life to a river that is never the same twice?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The image captures continuity and change at once, since the river is one yet always new.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the river of change. Identity and flux can coexist, as with a stream that is both itself and different.
items.lessonContent:
Continuity and change can coexist.
Images communicate abstract ideas.
Use metaphor to see, then look past it.
Hold both sameness and flux.
Share this: notice one thing that is continuous and changing at once.

items.title: Upside of Flux
items.question: What positive opportunity does impermanence offer for difficult states?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Because all things change, even hard states are not final, which is a reason for hope.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the gift of impermanence. The very fact that things change means suffering also has an end.
items.lessonContent:
Change works in both directions.
Painful states are not permanent either.
Hope follows from flux.
Remember transience in hard moments.
Share this: recall one difficulty that eventually changed.

items.title: Flowing Awareness
items.question: What does the teaching of change imply about the self or personality?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. If all conditioned things change, the self is better seen as an ongoing process than a fixed thing.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the self is a process. This need not mean there is no person, only that the person is not a frozen object.
items.lessonContent:
Persons can be processes, not objects.
Change applies inward as well as outward.
Reject frozen pictures of identity.
Notice how you differ from your past self.
Share this: name one way your sense of self has shifted over time.
